name: startup-applied-os-sandbox
what: OS-level confinement is real and applied once, irreversibly, at process start. The crate's module doc states it provides kernel-enforced sandboxing via nono (Landlock on Linux, Seatbelt on macOS) applied once at process startup, covering in-process `tokio::fs` calls and child processes, with process-level network deliberately left open because the agent needs the LLM API while child network is blocked per-subprocess via seccomp (xai-grok-sandbox/src/lib.rs:8-15). `SandboxManager::apply` resolves the profile, computes a capability set, applies it through `Sandbox::apply`, and then stores global state with an `applied` flag (lib.rs:179-262). The reverse direction is also implemented: `should_auto_allow_bash()` requires BOTH the `auto_allow_bash` setting AND `is_active()`, so sandbox state feeds the approval model rather than the other way round (lib.rs:100-106).
invariants: `apply` is documented irreversible: there is no unapply path, and the process either comes up confined or comes up under a refusal exit.
Sandbox state is process-global and set once (`OnceLock<GlobalSandboxState>`); a second apply cannot silently replace it.
`should_auto_allow_bash` must keep its `is_active()` conjunct - auto-allowing bash without an active sandbox would be an unconfined auto-approval.
failurePolicy: mixed - by itself `SandboxManager::apply` degrades gracefully (an unsupported platform or a failed apply logs, records and returns Ok while leaving `applied = false`, lib.rs:196-240); the fail-closed decision is taken by the caller, which refuses to start (see the next mechanism).

constants.name: enforce feature
constants.value: on by default; without it the crate is helpers-only and nothing is kernel-enforced

name: refuse-to-start-unprotected-sandbox
what: The startup path is explicitly fail-closed, and it is a five-way decision rather than a boolean. `apply_sandbox` lives in the shell (it is not in the sandbox crate) and its Linux branch routes through `route_bwrap_startup`, whose variants are ReexecRequired, ReexecOptional, Verify, Refuse and Continue (xai-grok-shell/src/config/mod.rs:1458-1469). ReexecRequired execs bubblewrap and, if the exec fails, prints `Refusing to start with denied paths unprotected.` and exits 1 (mod.rs:1527-1535). Verify is the anti-spoof arm: when the process reports being inside bwrap, the required hook write-deny, read-deny and `/data` write-deny mounts are each independently re-verified, and any failure exits 1 with the message naming a `possible __GROK_INSIDE_BWRAP spoof` (mod.rs:1545-1579). Refuse covers the case where the required bwrap plan could not be prepared at all (mod.rs:1581-1587). After the Landlock/Seatbelt apply, a second independent gate refuses startup when a profile that needs protection (`is_custom || needs_hooks`) did not actually get applied (mod.rs:1591-1626).
invariants: The `__GROK_INSIDE_BWRAP` marker is never trusted on its own - `trust_bwrap_marker_for_devbox()` is hardcoded false and the Verify arm re-checks the mounts.

The set of profiles that 'require' read-deny is computed intrinsically from the profile config, not from the resolved deny set, because the resolved set is empty on error and keying on it would silently downgrade to fail-open (lib.rs:441-467).

`resolve_failure_must_refuse` composes hook-write-deny OR read-deny OR data-write-deny, so a deny-carrying custom profile extends-devbox is covered by the read-deny arm even though the hook arm does not cover it (lib.rs:497-506).
Bwrap exec failure is fatal only when requires_bwrap; otherwise it is a warning and Landlock is the fallback.
failurePolicy: fail-closed - the process calls std::process::exit(1) rather than continuing unprotected; the only degrade path is an optional-bwrap profile, which warns and falls back to Landlock.

constants.name: refusal message
constants.value: "Refusing to start with denied paths unprotected."

name: predefined-sandbox-profiles-and-anti-hollowing-merge
what: Confinement is expressed as named profiles with a fixed built-in set - `workspace` (the default), `devbox`, `read-only`, `strict`, `off` - plus `Custom(name)` resolved from `~/.grok/sandbox.toml` or `.grok/sandbox.toml` (xai-grok-sandbox/src/profiles.rs:1-3, :69-112). A profile resolves to a `SandboxProfile` with read_only, read_write, deny, write_deny, default_read and restrict_network (profiles.rs:26-43), and read-deny is kernel-enforced on both platforms via the `deny` list (profiles.rs:3). The layering is deliberately not last-write-wins: the project config is additive only and is merged with `entry(name).or_insert(profile)`, so a workspace cannot redefine a profile name that already exists globally, because doing so would let a malicious workspace hollow out a user or enterprise profile while keeping the trusted name - emptying `deny` or broadening `read_write` (profiles.rs:114-167). Divergence is not silently ignored either: `sandbox_profile_conflicts` reports project profile names whose definition differs from the global one (profiles.rs:138-160). Only `read-only` and `strict` restrict child network by default (profiles.rs:80-84).
invariants: A project `.grok/sandbox.toml` can only ADD profile names; it can never replace a globally-defined profile's body.
The global config is read from `$GROK_HOME`, and the project path is workspace-relative - the two are never swapped.

`/dev/tty` may be dropped from the device set when it exists but cannot be opened (ENXIO without a controlling terminal), because a failed PathFd materialization aborts the whole Landlock ruleset - and that drop was itself the cause of a prior silent sandbox bypass under setsid/CI/headless launches (profiles.rs:183-200).
failurePolicy: fail-closed on policy composition (a conflicting project definition is ignored, keeping the trusted global body) and fail-soft on device enumeration (unopenable device nodes are skipped rather than aborting the ruleset); an unparsable sandbox.toml warns and is treated as absent (profiles.rs:169-181).

name: bwrap-reexec-with-read-deny-placeholders
what: On Linux a second, mount-level confinement layer is built as a bubblewrap re-exec. `bwrap_reexec_command_ex` composes a command that drops all capabilities (`--cap-drop ALL`), binds `/` through, mounts each deny_write path read-only, and - the interesting part - makes deny_READ paths unreadable by binding a mode-000 placeholder over them, since a read-only bind would still permit reading (xai-grok-sandbox/src/lib.rs:302-369, :385-428). The placeholder is suffixed with the current PID precisely because a shared path races between concurrent grok processes and a lost race could return None, silently dropping the bind and failing open (lib.rs:394-401). If a placeholder for a deny-read path cannot be created, the function prints `refusing to start with a partial sandbox` and returns None rather than emitting a bwrap command with that deny missing (lib.rs:333-344). A containment sentinel directory is also bound in, which is what the `__GROK_INSIDE_BWRAP` verification later checks for (lib.rs:345-352).
invariants: Read-deny requires a bind-over of an unreadable placeholder; a `--ro-bind` of the real path would be useless as a read denial.
The deny-read placeholder path must be PID-suffixed - sharing it across processes reintroduces the fail-open race.
A partial plan must abort: returning a bwrap command that silently omits one deny is the failure mode this code is written to avoid.
failurePolicy: fail-closed at plan construction (any missing placeholder or unencodable handoff returns None with an explanation, and the caller's Refuse arm exits 1); Windows/macOS compile to a None return since the path is Linux-only.

name: hook-write-deny-under-sandbox
what: The sandbox protects the hook installation path itself, closing the obvious escalation of writing a hook file to gain code execution on the next event. The crate exposes `requires_hook_write_deny` and the shell's startup calls `xai_grok_config::ensure_grok_hook_slots` before applying, failing the whole apply with `hook write-deny ensure failed` if the slots cannot be prepared (xai-grok-sandbox/src/lib.rs:50-64, :187-190). `SandboxManager::apply` also calls `maybe_install_namespace_lockdown_inside_bwrap` (lib.rs:191-192), and the module's own doc notes that shell fails closed when protection cannot be applied (lib.rs:50-51). `profile_enforces_hook_write_deny` and `verify_hook_write_deny_enforced` are re-exported so the startup path can both decide and then confirm the mounts took (lib.rs:39). `xai-grok-sandbox/src/hook_write_deny.rs` (415 lines) holds the plan builder, and the bwrap plan binds rootward ancestors read-write before the leaf read-only, with the ancestor ordering pinned by a test.
invariants: hook write-deny is verified after apply, not merely requested - and re-verified again in the shell's Verify arm.
The bwrap plan must RW-bind rootward ancestors before RO-binding the leaf; reversing the order would re-expose the hook directory.
A replaced leaf identity (the directory moved and recreated) must make append refuse, not silently bind the new one.
failurePolicy: fail-closed - an ensure failure aborts apply, an unenforced verification exits 1 at startup, and a plan that cannot be built returns None so the caller refuses.

name: permission-mode-projection-and-queue-drain
what: The approval model is one enum projected onto one boolean. `PermissionModeKind` has Default, Ask, Auto and AlwaysApprove, and AlwaysApprove is the only variant that projects to the shell's `yolo_mode = true`, with the canonical strings default/ask/auto/always-approve as the persisted vocabulary (xai-grok-pager/src/app/actions.rs:951-979). Switching always-approve ON drains the entire pending permission queue, answering each outstanding ACP RequestPermission with AllowOnce and falling back to Cancelled - never AllowAlways - and the flag flip is deliberately ordered before the drain (xai-grok-pager/src/app/dispatch/modes.rs:284-317). Auto is gated separately by `app.auto_mode_gate`: a commit to Auto degrades to Ask when the gate is off, and a display-side downgrade clears the per-agent auto flag so no badge can read Auto while it is disabled (modes.rs:408-420, :213-232). The enabled path also routes through a managed-policy refusal (`yolo_enable_blocked` / `refuse_if_yolo_locked`) before any state mutation (modes.rs:189-204, :353-399).
invariants: AllowOnce and never AllowAlways is the drain rule: enabling bypass must not mint a durable grant for whatever happened to be pending.
The mode flag is flipped before the queue is drained - reversing that ordering would let a permission racing the drain be answered under the old mode.
A commit to Auto must be downgraded, not rejected, when auto_mode_gate is off, and the displayed badge must be downgraded too so the UI cannot disagree with the engine.
failurePolicy: fail-closed with a soft projection - the gate either refuses the mode change outright (managed policy lock) or degrades Auto to Ask; pending requests are always answered (AllowOnce or Cancelled), so nothing is left hanging.

name: hooks-as-fail-open-gates-with-deny-precedence
what: Hooks act as permission gates on tool use, prompt submission and stop, with a documented fail-open posture and a strict decision precedence. `pre_tool_use` hooks can allow, ask or deny and can rewrite the tool input through `updatedInput`; prompt and stop gates can block; and the crate doc states the posture directly - fail-open by default, a hook error never blocks (xai-grok-hooks/src/lib.rs:11-17). The precedence is implemented as a match over accumulated per-hook outcomes and is total: a GateBlock yields Deny, otherwise a pending ask yields Ask, otherwise a deferring hook yields Defer, otherwise Allow (xai-grok-hooks/src/dispatcher.rs:316-326). The fail-open rule is called out as a security comment at the sequential gate: a hook that errors contributes nothing, and only a healthy deny blocks (dispatcher.rs:77). Distinct gate kinds get distinct timeouts rather than one global value: `DEFAULT_TIMEOUT_SECS = 5` for observe and tool gates, `DEFAULT_VERIFICATION_GATE_TIMEOUT_SECS = 600` for stop and post-tool gates because they run builds and linters, and `DEFAULT_PROMPT_GATE_TIMEOUT_SECS = 30` because a prompt gate runs before every prompt and a stuck hook would stall the session (xai-grok-hooks/src/config.rs:122-135, :168-178). Session-end hooks get their own bounded budget with a hard ceiling: default 1500 ms, maximum 60000 ms, and an out-of-range env value warns and falls back rather than applying (config.rs:137-166). A `timeout: 0` in a hook's config floors to the event default rather than disabling the bound (config.rs:608-609).
invariants: Fail-open is the stated default and is enforced by the sequential gate discarding errored hook results; a change that made a crashing hook block would invert the documented posture.
Precedence is Deny > Ask > Defer > Allow and is expressed as one exhaustive match, so no ordering of hook registration can promote an allow over an ask.
Timeout zero means 'use the event default', never 'no bound'.
The session-end budget has a hard maximum; the env var can raise the default up to the ceiling but not past it.
failurePolicy: fail-open on hook faults (an erroring or timing-out hook contributes nothing) but fail-closed on hook decisions (a healthy deny with exit code 2 blocks regardless of JSON); the combination means only a positive, successful deny stops a call.

name: retention-and-secret-redaction
what: Secret redaction is a code capability applied before values leave the process. `xai-grok-secrets` exposes a sanitizer surface rather than a policy: `redact_json_string_values`, `redact_secrets`, `redact_url`, `redact_user_paths` and a `walk_json_strings` traversal used to apply redaction across a JSON document (xai-grok-secrets/src/lib.rs:1-6). URL and user-path redaction are separate functions, so a URL that embeds a credential and a path that embeds a username are handled by different rules. The crate is classified as `safety` by the module checklist's keyword hint; from the code it is a data-handling capability that happens to sit in the credentials family.
invariants: Redaction walks string values rather than whole documents, so a structured value cannot be missed because it sits inside a nested object.
URL and path redaction are distinct entry points - collapsing them would either over-redact paths or under-redact URLs with embedded credentials.
failurePolicy: fail-soft - redaction is a pure transformation with no I/O and no error path (the exported functions return the redacted value), so its guarantee depends entirely on call-site coverage.

name: root-owned-managed-policy-pin
what: Deployment policy enters as a separate, higher-authority config layer rather than as a setting the user can flip back. Requirements load from unordered-on-disk but strictly-ordered layers: the user-writable `$GROK_HOME/requirements.toml` first, then the root-owned system file from `system_config_dir()`, then the macOS MDM managed-preferences layer last so it wins the deep merge - and the MDM layer is marked `is_system` exactly like the root-owned file (xai-grok-config/src/validation.rs:63-95). `is_system` is a stored flag rather than a re-derivation, with the stated reason that the source path is `GROK_HOME`-influenced and could carry `..` (validation.rs:56-58). `load_merged_requirements` deep-merges user then system so a user pin cannot win a conflict (validation.rs:97-106). The concrete user-facing effect is the always-approve lock: `[ui] disable_bypass_permissions_mode = true` in a requirements layer pins bypass off, with `[ui] yolo = false` kept as a back-compat alias, and the refusal string names the policy explicitly (xai-grok-workspace/src/permission/resolution.rs:918-932, :952, :1004).
invariants: Order is user -> root-owned system -> MDM, and later layers win; nothing may be inserted after the MDM layer.
Security decisions must read the stored `is_system` boolean, never re-derive it from the path.

The `fail_closed` key is stripped during normalization so it cannot deep-merge into the effective config and leak into a user config write; a regression test exists for exactly that (xai-grok-shell/tests/test_config_update_isolation.rs).
failurePolicy: fail-closed - `fail_closed = true` in a requirements layer turns an invalid `[[version_overrides]]` for this build into a startup error (RequirementsError::InvalidVersionOverrides) rather than a skipped layer, and an unreadable requirements.toml is treated as fail_closed armed (xai-grok-config/src/managed_cache.rs:180-194).

name: macos-mdm-forced-managed-preferences
what: On macOS an additional admin layer arrives through OS managed preferences rather than a file, and it is deliberately strong: `RequirementsSource::Mdm` is a distinct variant with no path at all, precisely so a caller cannot call `exists()` on it or read it as a file, and its label is the synthetic source id `ai.x.grok:...` (xai-grok-config/src/validation.rs:32-49). The layer is normalized through the same path as every other source and pushed last, and it is marked `is_system` so security decisions trust it like the root-owned layer (validation.rs:84-93). `managed_requirements_from` gates the whole thing on the forced read returning Some: a read that fails, or a value that is not valid base64, yields None - the layer is absent rather than partially applied (xai-grok-config/src/macos_managed.rs:22-29, :167-173). MDM is also a source for the sandbox-mode allow list, read through CoreFoundation and deliberately not environment-expanded.
invariants: The MDM layer has no filesystem path by construction; code that wants to inspect it must match on the enum, not build a PathBuf.
MDM is pushed after the root-owned system file so it wins the merge; the doc comment states this as the reason for its position.
A failed or unparsable forced read must produce no layer at all, not a partially-decoded one.
failurePolicy: fail-closed in effect - a broken MDM read removes the admin layer rather than installing a wrong one, but because the layer is admin-forced this also means policy is absent; the read itself is gated on an explicit `Some`.

name: ed25519-signed-policy-at-rest-fail-closed-arm
what: The cloud-cached requirements file is signed at rest once a key is embedded, and the managed cache carries an explicit armed state. `signed_policy.rs` treats a signed-ABSENT slot as requiring the file to be empty on disk, with the stated reason that a locally planted `requirements.toml` - the highest-precedence layer - is tamper and not noise (xai-grok-config/src/signed_policy.rs:375-389). The cache exposes `fail_closed_policy_armed_at`, which returns true when the sync marker records `fail_closed`, OR the on-disk requirements.toml parses as fail_closed, OR the file exists but is unreadable (managed_cache.rs:180-194). The unreadable case logs `requirements.toml unreadable; treating as fail_closed armed` and takes the armed branch.
invariants: A signed-absent slot must be empty on disk; non-empty content there is tamper, not a normal unverifiable state.
Unreadable is treated the same as fail_closed-armed - the failure mode of a permission error must not be 'policy off'.
There are three independent ways to be armed (marker, parsed flag, unreadable file); removing any one narrows the arming surface.
failurePolicy: fail-closed - an unreadable or tampered policy file arms fail-closed rather than disabling policy.

name: requirement-pinned-feature-flags-with-seven-tier-ladder
what: Every boolean `[features]` key resolves through one table-driven path in which the requirements tier outranks everything else. `Feature::resolve` chains the tiers and `resolve_bool_flag` returns them in a fixed order - requirement, cli, env, config, managed, remote/feature-flag, then the compiled default - so a requirements pin wins in both directions and a user-writable layer can never re-enable what an admin disabled (xai-grok-config-types/src/registry.rs:296-304; src/flags.rs:107-135). The registry is a table of feature specs, each naming its key, config path, environment variable, default and optional remote projection, so adding a feature means adding a row rather than inventing a resolution path (registry.rs:53-64, :86-240). Two knobs deliberately break out of the ladder and use bespoke resolvers because they are security-relevant: the egress gate walks mdm > system-requirements > user-requirements > managed > system-managed > user and has NO environment variable and NO remote tier at all, and the zero-data-retention access flag puts requirements first over env, config, managed and remote (xai-grok-shell/src/util/config/resolve/features.rs:7-24, :97-148).
invariants: The egress gate must exclude the config-overlay environment variable and campaign overlays from its walk, because it is an egress control and soft user-tier input must not be able to re-enable it.
That gate reads the layers first-match rather than the effective merged config, precisely because the merge puts user above managed - reading the merge would invert the intended precedence.
On a config-load error the requirements and managed tiers must still be consulted, so a corrupt user file cannot drop a policy pin.
A requirement pin must win in both directions: it can neither be overridden upward by a user nor downward by an absent value.
failurePolicy: mixed - the egress gate fails OPEN on genuinely absent policy (it defaults to enabled), and the user config tier is fail-open by design, while a requirement pin always wins. The feature registry itself defaults per row with six rows deliberately defaulting OFF, including LSP tools, web fetch and write-file.

name: config-overlay-confinement-allowlist
what: The process-environment config overlay is confined by a fail-closed allowlist rather than trusted wholesale. Only a small fixed set of paths survives the overlay - model selection, features, one toolset field, the two web-search domain lists and four shell-environment-policy filter fields - and everything else is discarded before the overlay is applied (xai-grok-config/src/config_override.rs:106-132). A separate strip list removes security-relevant sections entirely from patch and campaign inputs: version overrides, campaigns, the auth provider and model providers for patches, plus the whole auth and vendor-config sections for campaigns (config_override.rs:77-98). Security gates that must not see overlay influence read a deliberately overlay-free view of the config instead (config_layers.rs:150-153).
invariants: The allowlist is the control, so a new overlay-settable path is a deliberate policy decision rather than an incidental one.
Auth, provider and version-override sections must stay stripped from campaign inputs, or a campaign could redirect authentication.
Security-sensitive readers must use the overlay-free view, not the effective config, so the overlay cannot influence a policy decision even for an allowlisted path.
failurePolicy: fail-closed - anything not explicitly allowlisted is dropped from the overlay rather than passed through.

constants.name: OVERLAY_ALLOW_PATHS
constants.value: models, features, toolset.bash.login_shell_capture, two web-search domain lists, four shell_environment_policy filter fields

name: build-provenance-folder-trust-gate
what: Whether a repository's project-scoped hooks, MCP servers, language servers and plugins are allowed to load at all is decided by a folder-trust store, and that gate is itself disabled by build provenance rather than by configuration. `folder_trust_inert()` is defined as `is_local_build()`, which tests whether the version stamp was absent at compile time; the feature check short-circuits to false for a local build BEFORE reading any environment, config or managed value, with the stated reason that even an explicit opt-in is ignored so a self-built binary never prompts (xai-grok-workspace/src/folder_trust.rs:111-145). The release-stamped precedence is environment, then user config, then managed, then remote, defaulting to enabled (folder_trust.rs:151-157). Trust state lives in the user's grok home, never the repository, so a cloned repo cannot self-trust.
invariants: The trust store must live outside the repository: a cloned project cannot be allowed to add itself.
A runtime escape hatch treats a stamped version as a release build for test purposes; without it every test and CI run looks like a local build and the gate appears inert.
The build-provenance short-circuit must stay BEFORE any config read, or a local build could be made to prompt by setting an environment variable.
The hook disable check and its display counterpart must implement the same predicate, or the hooks interface misreports what will run.
failurePolicy: fail-closed for an untrusted folder in a release build (project hooks, MCP, LSP and plugins do not load) and deliberately inert in a local build (project scope always allowed, no store I/O at all).

name: managed-mcp-and-marketplace-denylists
what: Managed settings fold every managed-config and requirements layer plus a vendor managed-settings file into MCP-server and plugin-marketplace allow and deny policy, strictest-wins, and the layers are TIERED and sorted before application so a user-writable layer or the advisory vendor file can never claim a marketplace name or a policy pin's attribution ahead of an admin layer (xai-grok-workspace/src/permission/managed_policy/layer.rs:16-25; mod.rs:42-62, :125, :188-263). The server decision is deny-wins: any deny blocks, then a managed-only lockdown requires a positive allow-entry grant, then every binding restricted source must allow (managed_policy/mcp.rs:353-366). Marketplace blocking happens at the add path, failing with a named error rather than silently skipping (xai-grok-pager/src/plugin_cmd.rs:875-880).
invariants: An unknown or non-inspectable MCP transport is restricted by EVERY entry, so a future transport variant cannot slip past a lockdown.
An ambiguous policy subject origin must classify as foreign, which is the fail-closed direction.
Name matching is exact equality after normalization, never substring, and an empty key never matches.
Grants are deliberately authority-blind while restrictions are not - the asymmetry is intentional and must not be smoothed away.
failurePolicy: mixed but deny-biased - a layer whose config-to-JSON conversion fails is skipped and its pins are NOT applied, which is a genuine fail-open path on a malformed layer, while a dropped marketplace entry warns rather than silently allowing.

name: external-auth-provider-and-api-key-lockout
what: A deployment can replace the vendor's own authentication with an operator-supplied binary, and can lock out API-key authentication entirely. The provider is a command whose stdout carries the token, stderr the user-facing output and exit zero the success signal; the interactive path runs it with a five-minute timeout, while a headless mid-session refresh gets a much shorter budget (xai-grok-shell/src/auth/config.rs:64-66; src/auth/flow.rs:176-245; src/auth/external_auth.rs:42-44). The lockout knob `disable_api_key_auth` makes the API-key method neither advertised nor accepted, and the predicate ORs three independent sources - the config knob, the presence of a forced-login-team pin, and a call-time environment read - so a lower-trust user config cannot turn it back off (config.rs:74-77, :173-181). A login-principal check rejects a token whose team is not in the allowed set, and an empty allowed list fails closed (src/auth/oidc/protocol.rs:162-194).
invariants: A forced-login-team pin IMPLIES API-key auth is disabled, because team membership cannot be verified from a bare API key.
The client-side principal check is fail-fast UX and defence in depth, explicitly NOT the security boundary - the server re-validates the signed token, and the code says so.
The interactive provider run must not set the auth-expired environment variable, because operator binaries read it as 'headless, do not prompt'.
The lockout predicate must keep reading the environment at call time, or a long-lived process could miss an operator's change.
failurePolicy: mixed - a provider that fails or times out returns nothing and the flow falls back rather than persisting a partial credential, while the principal check and the API-key kill switch are fail-closed.

name: subscription-tier-and-zero-data-retention-gates
what: Two server-derived account gates share one classifier each. The subscription tier arrives as a free-form display string, and a single shared function classifies the personal free tier and the basic X tier as restricted while treating everything else - INCLUDING unknown future tier names - as unrestricted; the function exists so the cosmetic command gate and the engine's capability and toolset gate cannot drift apart (xai-grok-shell/src/tier.rs:6-19). Zero-data-retention is a separate pair of flags: a team-level check matches two blocked-reason markers, and a data-collection check ORs the coding-data retention opt-out (src/auth/model.rs:169-181). The rendered block is the conjunction of zero-data-retention and the access flag being off, and zero-data-retention hard-blocks sharing outright (xai-grok-pager/src/app/app_view.rs:1240-1242; xai-grok-shell/src/extensions/share.rs:49-50).
invariants: The shell treats a MISSING tier as unrestricted (fail-open, because the server is the authority on per-tier limits) while the pager treats absence as restricted (cosmetic, and it recovers on the next settings update) - the two postures differ deliberately and the difference is documented at the classifier.
An unknown tier name must stay unrestricted, so a new server-side tier does not gate every user until the client is updated.
Zero-data-retention flags arrive through a background user merge and must survive a credential refresh.
failurePolicy: mixed - fail-open on unknown tier names and fail-closed on the zero-data-retention gate, which blocks the session until the access flag is on.

constants.name: GROK_ZDR_ACCESS_ENABLED
constants.value: env override for the zero-data-retention access flag

name: enterprise-proxy-ca-bundle
what: Extra TLS roots for an enterprise proxy are opt-in through a dedicated environment variable with a fallback to the conventional certificate-file variable, and an explicitly EMPTY value disables both (xai-grok-extra-ca/src/lib.rs:14-18, :187-209). A bundle is read under a hard byte cap, PEM-parsed, and every certificate is X.509-validated through a throwaway root store before being added (lib.rs:275-326). Every client pins rustls with built-in webpki roots and the OS store enabled, and a default crypto provider is installed first-wins.
invariants: An explicitly empty value must disable the bundle, because the conventional certificate-file variable is frequently set process-wide by package managers and hermetic build tools - honoring it implicitly would silently change trust roots.
A bad bundle must never fail client construction; unparsable OS roots are likewise filtered so one bad root cannot break every client.
Every client must pin rustls, or feature unification can select a different TLS backend whose untyped errors break the certificate classifier.
failurePolicy: fail-soft throughout - an unreadable, oversized, block-less or zero-certificate bundle warns and contributes zero extra roots while the client is still built.
